6504.text:
The headline numbers were good
- Q2 operating profit (OP) was ¥34.8bn (+41% YoY), 5% above the ¥33.09bn Koyfin consensus.
- Full-year OP guidance rose from ¥156.5bn to ¥168.0bn, 4% above consensus (¥160.9bn).
- The dividend went up: interim ¥110 (from ¥107), year-end ¥130, full year ¥240 (+¥40).
- The balance sheet is now net cash, and first-half free cash flow was ¥58bn.

1. The beat was smaller and lower quality than it looks.
- Against Fuji’s own first-half guidance, OP beat by only ¥1.8bn (598 vs 580). ¥0.7bn of that was currency, so the underlying beat was ¥1.1bn, or about 2%.
First-half sales were ¥0.7bn below plan. Excluding currency, the shortfall was about ¥5.6bn.
- Segment, 1H vs company plan	: Sales/OP/OP excl. currency
Energy (data centres, grid):	−¥5.1bn (plant projects delayed)/−¥0.1bn/flat
Industry (factory components):	+¥3.3bn/+¥1.4bn/+¥1.4bn
Semiconductor:	+¥3.0bn/	+¥0.4bn/	−¥0.3bn
Food Distribution	−¥1.7bn/ +¥0.1bn	/—
- So Energy, the data-centre story the stock is priced on, only met its plan, and its sales slipped. The whole underlying beat came from Industry components.
- Management admitted in the Q&A that Q1 included pre-buying ahead of the June price rises (駆け込み需要), and that customers are placing orders “in anticipation” (先を見越した発注). Bears read that as double-ordering near a cycle peak.
- Fuji also said raw material prices settling “slightly more than expected” helped profit versus plan. That isn’t structural.

2. Growth is slowing, and the market trades the slowdown.

	First half	Second-half guidance
OP growth YoY	+40% / +15% (+20% excl. currency)
	Q1	Q2
Order growth YoY	+27% / +18%
Energy order increase YoY	+¥90bn / +¥64bn
Book-to-bill (orders ÷ sales)	1.56× / 1.28×
Orders are still strong, but the rate of change is falling.
FA component orders fell from Q1 to Q2. An analyst asked why they were weak relative to the market; management blamed one customer’s bulk order in Q1.
Fuji also moved the quarterly component-orders chart out of the presentation and into an Excel appendix, in the same quarter that metric weakened. That may be harmless, but it doesn’t look good.

3. Cracks in Asian data centres, and more reliance on one customer.

In July management called Thailand “particularly strong”. Now Thai projects are delayed by regulations, and Singapore has stopped growing.
Growth now rests on India and Australia, driven by one global data-centre customer (特定顧客).
Data-centre orders are still running about 2× last year, and FY sales will be “well above” the ¥100bn plan. But the story is more concentrated than it was.

4. Negative signals for FY3/28, beyond this year.

- Semiconductors: OP excluding currency fell more than ¥4bn in the first half. Price competition in China is “intensifying”.
Second-half automotive chip sales depend on customers taking contractually committed volumes.
For next year, management said customer inventory adjustments will continue and it is “not optimistic”.
- Energy: the second-half guidance builds in worse margins in power-plant projects because of project mix. Energy second-half sales need to be 1.55× the first half (last year 1.39×), while plant projects are already slipping. Energy also plans to add another 772 staff in the second half.
FY3/28 consensus OP is ¥180bn. Against the new ¥168bn base that is only about +7% growth, so the market is starting to price “peak growth”.

5. Management signalled less sandbagging, so less future upside.

President Kondo said better data analysis now lets Fuji forecast more accurately and it will “update the market agilely”.
This time the second half was raised by ¥9.7bn. Last year Fuji raised mainly the first half and left the second half almost unchanged. The guide is therefore closer to a true estimate.
The beat-and-raise pattern was the main source of upside surprise for the market, and for my own model. Management’s own quantified remaining upside is small:
- “Twenty-odd ¥bn of 億” (about ¥2bn+) if current exchange rates hold. The guidance still assumes ¥150/$.
- About ¥1bn+ from cost cuts.
That points to about ¥171–172bn for the year.

6. Capital returns: no buyback, and a modest ROE target.

- No buyback despite net cash and ¥58bn of first-half free cash flow.
- The ROE target of 15% by FY2030 is barely above where FY3/27 guidance puts ROE now (about 14%).
- Management said it will “accelerate growth investment” as the equity ratio rises, which raises the risk of spending on capex or M&A rather than returns. The new mid-term plan is about “shifting into growth areas”.
- Semiconductor capex jumps in the second half (¥13.1bn vs ¥5.3bn in the first) even as semiconductor profit falls 30%.

7. Net profit lagged operating profit.

- Full-year net profit was raised only ¥5.5bn against an OP raise of ¥11.5bn. Guided EPS of ¥800 is slightly below the ¥806 consensus.
- Two causes: currency losses and a loss provision at an overseas subsidiary, booked below OP; and minority interests doubling (¥2.76bn vs ¥1.25bn).
- My guess is that the minority jump reflects the 37% Schneider stake in the components subsidiary, where the price-driven boom is happening [EXTRAPOLATION]. If so, more than a third of the best-performing profit stream doesn’t reach Fuji’s shareholders.

8. Minor, but worth watching: Food Distribution.

- The cut to full-year guidance cites lower demand in store equipment as well as vending machines. In July, store equipment was growing.
- The 7-Eleven antitrust matter is now classified as a contingent liability; that’s the normal progression, not an escalation.
- Whether 7-Eleven has paused or re-tendered its orders is a question for IR [EXTRAPOLATION].

9. The market backdrop.

- The stock had already fallen 13% from ¥15,395 (6 Oct) to ¥13,385 before the results. That came amid an AI-related sell-off: the Nikkei fell 5% on 15 Oct after CoreWeave’s bonds dropped, and Meta fell 9% on its capex and cash-flow numbers.
- The results landed in the same week as Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon. I couldn’t verify how the market reacted to those overnight, so I can’t separate the sector effect from the stock-specific one.

# **KYOCERA FY27 1H SEGMENT FINANCIALS & FORWARD OUTLOOK**

**1\. Industrial Tools Unit** (Solutions Business) 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 106.8B (9.9% of tot) | OP JPY 19.2B (23.0% of tot) [Margin: 17.9%] 
• **2H Outlook:** Sales & profit expected to decline vs 1H. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** 1H boosted by pull-forward buying ahead of 3-round tungsten price hikes; 2H hit by full raw material cost increases.

**2\. Semiconductor Components Unit** (Core Components) 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 221.1B (20.5% of tot) | OP JPY 31.5B (37.7% of tot) [Margin: 14.2%] 
• **2H Outlook:** Lower 2H underlying profit; offset by \~JPY 15B Chemical Business sale gain. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** 1H smartphone package pull-forward; organic packages at full capacity; upside potential from AI market demand.

**3\. Electronic Components Business** 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 215.3B (20.0% of tot) | OP JPY 19.6B (23.5% of tot) [Margin: 9.1%] 
• **2H Outlook:** 2H performance may match or exceed 1H levels. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** Strong AI data center MLCC/capacitor demand & KAVX yield gains; solid inquiries extending into FY28.

**4\. Document Solutions Unit** (Solutions Business) 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 248.2B (23.0% of tot) | OP JPY 29.6B (35.5% of tot) [Margin: 11.9%] 
• **2H Outlook:** Demand & profit expected to moderate in 2H. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** Fading of non-recurring 1H US tariff refunds & customer pre-buys hedging memory cost increases.

**5\. Industrial & Automotive Components** (Core Components - SPE) 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 134.1B (12.4% of tot) | OP JPY 19.2B (23.0% of tot) [Margin: 14.3%] 
• **2H Outlook:** 2H upside potential from semiconductor processing equipment (SPE) demand. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** High SPE ceramic demand; Isahaya plant operational Spring 2027 (targeting JPY 25B/yr from FY31).

**6\. Communications Unit** (Solutions Business) 
• **1H Performance:** Sales JPY 106.9B (9.9% of tot) | OP JPY 7.9B (9.5% of tot) [Margin: 7.4%] 
• **2H Outlook:** Stable 2H seasonal trend execution. 
• **Drivers & Risks:** Ongoing business portfolio and cost structure optimization.
---
## *Total 1H Sales Revenue: JPY 1,078.3B | Total 1H Business Profit: JPY 83.5B*#\================================================================================ 

**KEY FORWARD GUIDANCE & STRATEGIC TAKEAWAYS**
• **Full-Year Guidance:** Sales revised **+JPY 40B to JPY 2.12T** on AI component demand; OP maintained at **JPY 160B**. 2H division estimates are framed as **"somewhat prudent."** 
• **Capital Expenditure:** Will be revised **upward** beyond initial peak plans due to sustained strong capacity requests. 
• **Collaboration & Risks:** JAE European sales transfer starts **Jan 2027** (manufacturing framework **1H FY28**); domestic tungsten recycling refinery opens in **FY31**. 
• **Portfolio & ROE:** Business portfolio reviews remain an ongoing discipline after JPY 29.5B GaN impairment; management maintains steady target of **8%+ ROE by FY31**.

8136.text:
Five issues.

1. North America is the most important near-term earnings swing factor. Management is maintaining its H2 recovery expectations, but the Q&A reveals that the business remains exposed to tariffs, licensee turnover and uneven retail shelf-space allocation. There are encouraging signs:
- Cinnamoroll and Kuromi each grew approximately 50% in Q1.
- Q1 US performance was better than initially expected.
- Character momentum remains strong according to retailers and Sanrio's sales teams.
However, the 18-month lead time for licensing agreements means new partnerships cannot immediately compensate for lost business. The 10% US market-share target is therefore a medium- to long-term ambition rather than something likely to be achieved quickly.

2. The Asia growth target looks demanding, with China the critical variable.
Asia royalty income grew only 3.5% in Q1 against a full-year target of 22.5%. Although management attributes some of the weakness to a ¥1bn timing difference, the underlying challenge remains significant. China needs to deliver, but Sanrio has not yet benefited from some of the content-related catalysts available elsewhere, notably the Netflix Kuromi animation and Alifish animation.
The key question is whether Sanrio can successfully diversify its Chinese licensing business beyond Hello Kitty.

3. Sanrio is consciously sacrificing some near-term margins for growth.
This is an important admission from management. Gaming has lower margins than licensing, and strategic project expenditure is increasing. Consequently, even if revenue grows, the overall domestic operating margin may not improve materially in the near term. Management appears comfortable with this trade-off because it believes gaming can ultimately increase character popularity and generate higher-margin licensing opportunities.
Investors should distinguish between:
- Temporary margin dilution associated with investments that generate future returns.
- Structural deterioration in margins resulting from higher operating costs or less profitable business mix.
The Q&A does not yet provide sufficient evidence to quantify the returns on these investments.

4. The international licensing model still has some concentration and sustainability risks.
Several examples illustrate this:
- Europe remains heavily dependent on apparel.
- South Korea's quarterly results can be heavily influenced by individual large licensing agreements.
- China remains heavily dependent on Hello Kitty.
- North America has exposure to licensee turnover and retailer shelf-space decisions.
Sanrio is clearly trying to diversify across characters, categories, customers and geographies. However, the 18-month licensing lead time means that diversification takes time to translate into financial results.

5. The conversion of brand popularity into actual consumer spending is the key long-term challenge.
The 7.1 million YouTube subscribers, growing non-Asian customer base in the US and strong character growth are encouraging indicators. But management itself acknowledges that social media awareness does not automatically translate into purchases. The next phase requires local sales teams, local brand partnerships, physical retail distribution and products that resonate with consumers in each market. This is an important distinction when assessing Sanrio: strong IP awareness is an asset, but the monetisation of that asset depends on distribution, licensing execution and consumer purchasing behaviour.

1. Forward-looking points
A. North America: H2 recovery is critical
- Management maintained its original expectation that North American sales could decline during H1, followed by a recovery in H2.
- Although Q1 sales in local currency increased, management said performance was broadly in line with expectations. Q1 was actually better than its initial expectations, thanks to sales initiatives.
- The operating environment remains volatile:
  - US tariffs continue to have an impact.
  - Some licensees have reduced retail shelf space, while others have expanded it.
  - There has been turnover among licensees.
- Management believes character popularity remains strong and its sales strategy is working.
- H2 growth is expected to be driven primarily by:
  - Continued momentum in Sanrio characters.
  - Greater promotion of characters beyond Hello Kitty.
  - Another major Kuromi campaign around Halloween.
  - Securing new licensing partners.
Character performance in Q1:
- Cinnamoroll: approximately 50% growth YoY.
- Kuromi: approximately 50% growth YoY.
Both remain relatively small businesses compared with Hello Kitty, but management views their growth as encouraging.
- Sanrio's US market share target is 10%.
- Management is confident in maintaining current momentum but does not expect a dramatic overnight increase in sales.
- Licensing deals typically take approximately 18 months from signing to generating sales, which limits the speed at which new partnerships can contribute.
B. Europe: diversifying beyond apparel
- European business remains heavily concentrated in apparel licensing.
- Management considers expansion into non-apparel categories particularly important to sustain growth and reduce reliance on apparel.
- Some apparel licensees experienced turnover in Q1, reinforcing the need to continually recruit new partners.
- Management has been engaging with prospective licensees for some time, and these efforts are beginning to bear fruit.
- The company does not expect a sudden deterioration in Q2, given continuing character momentum and the development of new partnerships.
- As in the US, the typical lead time between signing a licensing agreement and generating sales is approximately 18 months.
- By country:
  - UK is the largest European market by business scale.
  - Eastern Europe, Italy and Turkey are currently making notable contributions to growth.
- India is considered a potentially significant long-term opportunity, although management expects development to take time because of market instability and counterfeit/unauthorised products.
C. Asia: China is essential to achieving the full-year target
- Sanrio is forecasting 22.5% royalty income growth in Asia for FY2027, compared with only 3.5% growth in Q1.
- China is the most important market in achieving this target.
- Historically, the Chinese business has been heavily dependent on Hello Kitty. Management wants to extend this momentum to other characters.
- Unlike other markets, China has not benefited from:
  - The Netflix Kuromi animation, which is not available in China.
  - The Alifish animation, which has not yet launched.
- Sanrio is continuing to release content and develop partnerships with licensees that have strong brand value.
- Q2 has already ended, meaning delivery of the full-year growth target will depend on the ability to convert these initiatives into results from Q3 onwards.
- Management noted that Q1 growth was affected by a ¥1.0 billion timing difference in the prior-year comparison. Excluding this, underlying growth in Asia is considered solid.
- Expansion of the retail store network is another important initiative. Management hopes that stronger retail presence will increase character popularity and ultimately improve sell-through for licensees.
D. South Korea: growth remains deal-dependent
- Sanrio has a relatively high market share in South Korea.
- It has approximately 200 licensees, a number that has remained relatively stable.
- However, quarterly performance can be volatile because of the importance of large individual licensing deals.
- Recent examples:
  - Previous year's strong Q3 was boosted by a large cosmetics-related licensing deal.
  - Q1 FY2027 benefited from growth in digital games and a new Pompompurin licensing deal.
- Although South Korea is not particularly large in terms of Sanrio's overall business, it can be an important source of trends that influence other markets.
- K-beauty is one such example, although management explicitly stated that it does not currently see a strong connection between K-beauty's popularity in the US and Sanrio's US growth. US growth is currently coming more from apparel and toys than beauty.
E. Global brand development and customer acquisition
- Management believes overseas markets are particularly important for expanding Sanrio's customer base.
- The Hello Kitty & Friends YouTube channel has reached approximately 7.1 million subscribers.
- In the US:
  - Sanrio is gradually expanding beyond the East and West Coasts.
  - Its customer base is becoming more diverse, including more non-Asian consumers.
- In Europe, Sanrio characters are already being used by apparel brands with pan-European reach.
- However, management recognises that social media awareness does not automatically translate into purchases.
- The next phase involves collaborating with local brands so consumers develop a genuine connection with Sanrio characters.
- Management has formulated its strategy but needs to expand local sales teams and recruit more local sales personnel to execute it effectively.
Important distinction: Management believes awareness is already sufficiently established through social media in certain markets. The challenge is now converting awareness into actual consumer purchases.
F. Gaming and strategic investment
- Sanrio's first-party game was scheduled for release in October 2026.
- Marketing expenditure originally planned for Q1 has shifted into Q2.
- Sanrio will publish the game in Japan, while Bandai Namco handles publishing in North America and Europe.
- Sanrio bears the marketing costs in Japan, while Bandai Namco bears overseas marketing costs.
- The overseas revenue-sharing arrangement has not been disclosed, although management considers the terms broadly consistent with industry practice.
- Sanrio does not disclose unit sales forecasts.
- Management expects the game business to increase in importance over time, even though it carries relatively lower margins than licensing.
- In the medium to long term, greater character popularity generated through gaming is expected to create positive spillover effects for licensing.
G. Profit margins and investment spending
- Management warned that significantly improving domestic profit margins in the near term may be difficult.
- The Japan segment comprises:
  - Product sales.
  - Licensing.
  - Theme parks.
  - Other businesses.
- Licensing is particularly profitable, so an increase in its contribution raises overall margins.
- However, management expects licensing's weighting to decline in the near term as the company increases investment in the relatively lower-margin gaming business.
- Management is also increasing expenditure on projects supporting its long-term vision.
- Project-related expenses are the principal area where management has flexibility to adjust costs.
- Nevertheless, management believes this is the right time to invest and is deliberately increasing these expenditures.
H. Capital allocation and medium-term guidance
- Sanrio will no longer publish a medium-term management plan.
- Management is considering how best to communicate its capital allocation approach at the FY2027 full-year results briefing.
- This creates some uncertainty regarding the company's medium-term financial targets and capital allocation priorities.

2. Other points relating to recent results and business performance
A. Japan product sales: operating profit and margin pressure
- Q1 operating profit from product sales in Japan was ¥3.5bn, compared with ¥3.3bn in the same period last year.
- Despite the increase in operating profit, the operating profit margin declined YoY.
- Management identified two reasons:
  1. Higher personnel expenses: Sales growth in the previous year exceeded expectations, and stores lacked sufficient staffing capacity. Sanrio increased hiring, and the resulting higher personnel costs have now become part of its normal cost base.
  2. Shinsaibashi flagship store: The store opened at the end of July, but rent and other lease-related costs were already being incurred during Q1, before revenue generation began.
B. Japan licensing: Pompompurin particularly strong
- Pompompurin performed exceptionally well:
  - Product sales approximately doubled YoY.
  - Licensing results approximately doubled YoY.
- Miscellaneous goods continued to perform well, maintaining the trend seen in the previous year.
- However, management is conscious of the risk of overexposure in miscellaneous goods following significant growth since last year.
- The company is therefore trying to diversify both its character portfolio and product categories.
C. SG&A: ¥2bn of expenditure deferred from Q1
- Approximately ¥2bn of SG&A expenditure originally budgeted for Q1 was deferred.
- The expenditure relates to gaming marketing ahead of the first-party game launch in October.
- Management clarified that:
  - The expenditure was shifted from Q1 into Q2.
  - It was not an unnecessary budget allocation that ultimately went unspent.
  - The original intention had been to incur a significant portion of gaming-related SG&A in Q1, but the timing was subsequently refined.
- Management did not indicate that the full-year SG&A forecast would be exceeded.
- The apparent large YoY increase in Q1 SG&A was also partly due to a relatively low expense base in Q1 of the previous year.
D. North America: Q1 better than initial expectations, but H1 remains challenging
- Local-currency sales increased in Q1, despite the previously indicated expectation of a weak first half.
- Management said Q1 was better than its initial expectations, reflecting the effectiveness of sales initiatives.
- Nevertheless, management maintained its expectation of weaker performance across H1, including the possibility of a decline in Q2.
- The full-year outlook remained unchanged from the June announcement.
- Licensee turnover has not resulted in a material deterioration in sales so far, with stronger partners helping to offset weaker ones.
E. Asia: reported growth affected by timing differences
Indicator	Q1 FY2027 growth
Asia royalty income	+3.5% YoY
South Korea royalty income	Not separately quantified
Full-year Asia royalty income target	+22.5% YoY

- The Q1 Asia growth rate was relatively low partly because of a timing difference against the prior year.
- Management quantified this prior-year timing difference at approximately ¥1bn.
- Excluding this effect, management considers underlying Asia growth to be solid.
- The challenge is to accelerate growth from Q3 onwards to achieve the full-year target.
F. South Korea: individual licensing deals create volatility
- Previous-year Q3 performance benefited from a large cosmetics licensing deal.
- Q1 FY2027 performance benefited from:
  - Growth in digital games.
  - A new Pompompurin licensing agreement.
- Sanrio has approximately 200 licensees in South Korea, and the number is relatively stable.
- Nevertheless, a small number of large licensees and individual transactions can have a disproportionate impact on quarterly results.
- Management believes underlying character momentum remains strong.
G. Europe: existing apparel business and new partnerships
- Some apparel licensees experienced turnover during Q1.
- However, management believes that its efforts to secure replacement partners are beginning to generate results.
- The UK remains the largest European market by overall business scale.
- Eastern Europe, Italy and Turkey are making particularly notable contributions to growth.
- Management is confident that the business will not suddenly weaken in Q2, although it acknowledges the need to diversify beyond apparel.
H. US consumer demographics and brand penetration
- The Hello Kitty & Friends YouTube channel has approximately 7.1 million subscribers.
- Sanrio is seeing gradual expansion beyond the traditional East and West Coast US markets.
- Its customer base is becoming more diverse, with increasing engagement from non-Asian consumers.
- The Hello Kitty Café in Chicago was cited in the Q&A as an example of increasing non-Asian customer participation.
- However, management stressed that increased brand awareness has yet to translate fully into sales.

3. Key figures and milestones to monitor
Area	                        Current position / target	                                              What to monitor
Japan product sales	Q1 operating profit ¥3.5bn vs ¥3.3bn YoY	                Margin recovery as new stores mature
Pompompurin	        Product sales and licensing approximately 2x YoY	Sustainability and category diversification
Deferred SG&A	        ¥2bn shifted from Q1 to Q2	                                        Gaming marketing effectiveness
North America	        Q1 better than initial expectations	                                H2 recovery and licensee replacement
US market share	       10% target	                                                                        Progress in retail distribution and customer penetration
US character growth	Cinnamoroll and Kuromi ~50% YoY in Q1	                Whether momentum continues beyond seasonal campaigns
Licensing lead time	~18 months from signing to sales	                                Pipeline of new licensing agreements
Europe	                        UK largest market; Eastern Europe, Italy and Turkey key growth contributors	    Non-apparel diversification
Asia royalty income	Q1 +3.5%; FY target +22.5%	                                        Acceleration from Q3
China	                        Critical to Asia growth target	                                        Expansion beyond Hello Kitty and new licensing partnerships
South Korea	                ~200 licensees	                                                                Dependence on large individual deals
YouTube	                Hello Kitty & Friends ~7.1m subscribers	                        Conversion of online engagement into purchases
India	                        Long-term growth opportunity	                                        Market development and counterfeit-product issues

Main takeaways from results Q&A - watch for continued slowdown in China and US as business model shifts and consumption demand moderates due to inflation, plus higher SG&A going into next year’s launch of the Hollywood movie. There is also the investment in Harmonyland. But highest margins are in licensing. Expect margin deterioration nearer-term, eg. investments also going into gaming.

- Target mkt cap of Y5trn in 8 years vs. Y1.37trn now = 17.6% CAGR in share price. Is this achievable?
- Currently refining investment and capital allocation roadmap for the next 8 years. Abolished medium term plan. 
- 1H performance not better than expected.
- 2H: cut in SG&A for the year, in light of economic environment, means underspend of Y2bn SG&A in 1Q won’t be all spent in 2H. 2Q SG&A spend inline with budget. 1H SG&A Y39.5bn, FY Y89.1bn = 2H Y49.6bn.
- 2H expenditure incl: higher personnel costs, gaming marketing during yearend/New Year, character brand events in Japan and overseas, projects that support long-term vision. 
- Launch of FY2028 Hollywood film = pre-release licensing and sustained post-release monetisation. There will be upfront marketing ahead of the film’s release. Emphasis on measuring film ROI through incremental licensing revenue.
- China: Single digit licensing growth may be a reflection of change in strategy vs. weaker demand, also strong FY2026. Moving away from prioritising short-term licensing sales growth ie. it was chasing short-term growth, now focusing on selection of licensees to drive long term value of brands. Licensing managed by Alifish, on category-by-category basis. Broader macro concerns leading to fluctuations in demand is a concern.
- North America - getting more granular to establish IP as part of mainstream consumer culture: Inflation and weaker consumer sentiment means anticipated recover could be delayed until next FY ie. FY28, or beyond. Implementing more granular account management, segmenting customers by IP, demographic and distribution channel. Dedicated sales teams developing customised product designs and proposals for different categories. Major retailers have dedicated Sanrio teams. Strategy to secure retail shelf space throughout the year: the 4 seasons, back to school, and other seasonal occasions.  
- Theme park Puroland and Harmonyland: positioned as customer engagement platforms. Further scope to raise visitor numbers, there is a planned expansion of Harmonyland (USD66mn) soon, as of Dec 2025. Puroland avg spending per customer >Y10k, due to dynamic pricing of admission tickets and higher perceived value, theme-park exclusive products, higher F&B prices due to inflation. Merchandise sales at 20-30% of total customer spend at theme parks.
- Gaming: domestic sales following launch slightly below plan, overseas inline. Brand/title awareness insufficient. Gaming loss forecast for FY27 not changed significantly. Shortfall from domestic sales offset by other businesses. Goal of 10 titles by March 2029.
